question: Who are our top 10 customers by total spend?
sql: SELECT oi.user_id AS customer_id, u.state, u.country, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_spend, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY total_spend DESC LIMIT 10
report:
**Top customers by net spend (all time, cancelled and returned items excluded).**
- The top 10 customers each spent between $1.36k and $1.95k; the #1 customer (id 54086, Beijing) spent $1,948 across 3 orders.
- Top customers are *not* frequent buyers: most placed 2-4 orders. Their value comes from high basket size (AOV $340-$1,390 vs. a company average of ~$86), i.e. a few premium items (outerwear, suits).
- They are geographically spread (China, South Korea, France, US, Germany, Brazil): no single market concentrates our high-value buyers.
**Interpretation rules used:** spend = SUM(order_items.sale_price) for items not Cancelled/Returned; customers identified only by pseudonymous id plus city/state/country (never names or contact details).
**Action items:** (1) build a VIP segment on AOV > $300 for premium launches; (2) test a second-purchase incentive since even top customers rarely exceed 3 orders.
author: analytics-team

question: What is our monthly revenue trend over the last 12 months?
sql: WITH monthly AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS month, ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders FROM order_items WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 12 MONTH)) GROUP BY 1) SELECT month, revenue, orders, ROUND(revenue / orders, 2) AS aov, ROUND(100 * SAFE_DIVIDE(revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)), 1) AS mom_growth_pct FROM monthly ORDER BY month
report:
**Monthly net revenue, last 12 full months + month-to-date.**
- Revenue grew from $191.6k (Oct 2025) to $415.9k (Sep 2026), +117% in 11 months; growth accelerated from May 2026 (+18% MoM) and peaked in Sep 2026 (+20.7% MoM).
- Growth is volume-driven: orders went from 2,137 to 5,009 while AOV stayed flat around $83-$89.
- **Caveat:** the current month (Oct 2026) shows -43.6% MoM only because it is partial. Never compare a partial month with a full one: compare month-to-date against the same number of days of the previous month, or exclude the current month.
**Interpretation rules used:** net revenue = SUM(sale_price) excluding Cancelled and Returned items; month = DATE_TRUNC(created_at, MONTH); MoM via LAG().
author: analytics-team

question: Compare the performance of Calvin Klein and Levi's. Why do they perform differently?
sql: SELECT p.brand, COUNT(*) AS items_sold, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_price, ROUND(100 * (1 - SUM(p.cost) / SUM(oi.sale_price)), 1) AS gross_margin_pct, ROUND(100 * COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_rate_pct, COUNT(DISTINCT p.id) AS active_skus, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT p.id), 2) AS revenue_per_sku FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE p.brand IN ('Calvin Klein', 'Levi\'s') AND oi.status != 'Cancelled' GROUP BY 1
report:
**Calvin Klein vs Levi's (all time, cancelled items excluded).**
| Metric | Calvin Klein | Levi's |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $171.7k | $65.7k |
| Items sold | 2,685 | 1,249 |
| Avg selling price | $63.95 | $52.64 |
| Gross margin | 53.2% | 49.7% |
| Return rate | 11.4% | 11.0% |
| Active SKUs | 495 | 255 |
| Revenue per SKU | $347 | $258 |
**Why they differ:** the gap (2.6x revenue) decomposes into (1) **assortment breadth**: CK has ~2x the SKUs; (2) **productivity per SKU**: each CK SKU earns 35% more, driven by (3) **price**: CK sells at a 21% higher average price with a 3.5pt better margin. Returns are not a differentiator (11.4% vs 11.0%).
**Method:** decompose revenue = SKUs x revenue/SKU, and revenue/SKU = price x units; always check return rate and margin before concluding a brand is "better".
**Action items:** expand Levi's assortment only in categories where its revenue/SKU is at parity; review Levi's pricing vs CK in overlapping categories (Jeans, Pants).
author: analytics-team

question: Why are users in Texas underspending compared to users in California?
sql: WITH customer_spend AS ( SELECT oi.user_id, u.state, u.age, u.traffic_source, SUM(oi.sale_price) AS spend, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') AND u.state IN ('Texas', 'California') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4) SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(AVG(spend), 2) AS avg_spend_per_customer, ROUND(AVG(orders), 2) AS avg_orders_per_customer, ROUND(SUM(spend) / SUM(orders), 2) AS aov, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) AS avg_age, ROUND(100 * COUNTIF(traffic_source = 'Search') / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_search FROM customer_spend GROUP BY 1
report:
**Texas vs California customers (net spend, all time).**
- The premise does not hold: Texas customers spend *slightly more* per head ($120.97 vs $117.73) with the same frequency (1.41 orders each) and a higher AOV ($85.49 vs $83.41).
- California's *total* is larger only because it has 55% more customers (2,455 vs 1,581). "Underspending" at state level is a **reach** issue, not a **wallet** issue.
- Demographics and acquisition mix are near-identical (avg age 41 vs 40.5; ~69-70% acquired via Search), so no segment explains a difference.
**Interpretation rules used:** always separate total spend into customers x spend per customer x frequency before explaining a gap; check composition (age, channel) before claiming behavioural differences.
**Action items:** treat Texas as an acquisition opportunity (grow customer count) rather than a monetisation problem.
author: analytics-team

question: Why did our churn rate spike last month?
sql: WITH activity AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS month FROM orders WHERE status != 'Cancelled'), months AS (SELECT DISTINCT month FROM activity WHERE month >= DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 6 MONTH)), base AS ( SELECT m.month, a.user_id FROM months m JOIN activity a ON a.month BETWEEN DATE_SUB(m.month, INTERVAL 3 MONTH) AND DATE_SUB(m.month, INTERVAL 1 MONTH) GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT b.month, COUNT(DISTINCT b.user_id) AS active_prev_3m, COUNT(DISTINCT IF(a.user_id IS NULL, b.user_id, NULL)) AS not_returning, ROUND(100 * COUNT(DISTINCT IF(a.user_id IS NULL, b.user_id, NULL)) / COUNT(DISTINCT b.user_id), 1) AS churn_rate_pct FROM base b LEFT JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.month = b.month GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
report:
**Customer churn, monthly.**
Definition (agreed with Finance): a customer is *at risk/churned in month M* if they ordered in the 3 months before M but not in M. Churn rate = churned / active in the prior 3 months.
- Baseline churn is structurally high (92-96%): most customers buy once or twice, so monthly "churn" mostly reflects purchase frequency, not lost customers. It *improved* steadily from 95.8% (Apr) to 91.8% (Sep 2026).
- The "spike" to 97.4% this month is an artifact: the month is not over, so many customers simply haven't ordered *yet*. Re-measure on a complete month, or compare against the same day-of-month in prior months.
- For a real spike, check (1) the cohort that drove it (first-time vs repeat buyers), (2) return/cancel rate in the prior month, (3) fulfilment delays.
**Action items:** report churn on complete months only; add a 90-day repeat-purchase KPI which is more meaningful for this business.
author: analytics-team

question: Create a report for Q1 including insights and action items for Q2
sql: SELECT p.category, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS q1_revenue, ROUND(100 * (1 - SUM(p.cost) / SUM(oi.sale_price)), 1) AS gross_margin_pct, ROUND(100 * COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_rate_pct, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.user_id) AS customers FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.status != 'Cancelled' AND DATE(oi.created_at) BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY q1_revenue DESC LIMIT 10
report:
**Q1 2026 Category Performance Report (Jan 1 - Mar 31, cancelled items excluded).**
*Executive summary:* Outerwear & Coats led Q1 revenue ($97.7k) at a strong 55.7% margin; Jeans was #2 in revenue ($79.5k) and #1 in customers (787) but carries the weakest margin among the leaders (46.6%).
*Insights:*
1. Revenue concentrates in seasonal categories (Outerwear, Sweaters): expect Q2 seasonality to shift mix to Swim/Shorts.
2. Margin leaders are Suits & Sport Coats (59.9%) and Active (57.9%): high-margin but mid-volume.
3. Returns are uniform (10.7%-13.3%), highest in Tops & Tees (13.3%) and Suits (13.1%).
*Action items for Q2:*
- Shift marketing from Outerwear to Swim and Shorts ahead of the season; protect Swim margin (49.1%) by limiting discounting.
- Grow Active (57.9% margin) with targeted campaigns to existing Jeans buyers.
- Investigate Tops & Tees returns (sizing guides, product photos).
*Format rules:* executive summary first, 3-5 numbered insights with the number that proves each, then owner-ready action items.
author: analytics-team

question: Which categories have the highest return rates and how much revenue do returns cost us?
sql: SELECT p.category, COUNT(*) AS items_sold, ROUND(100 * COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_rate_pct, ROUND(SUM(IF(oi.status = 'Returned', oi.sale_price, 0)), 2) AS returned_revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.status != 'Cancelled' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY return_rate_pct DESC LIMIT 10
report:
**Returns by category (all time, cancelled items excluded).**
- Return rates are tightly clustered (11.8%-12.7%): Tops & Tees highest at 12.7%. No category is an outlier, so returns are a **systemic** issue (sizing/fit policy) rather than a product-specific one.
- In dollars, the cost concentrates in high-price categories: Outerwear & Coats ($135.7k returned) and Jeans ($123.8k) dwarf Tops & Tees ($53.7k) despite lower rates.
**Interpretation rules used:** rank by *returned revenue* for business impact, by *rate* for quality signals; return rate = Returned items / non-cancelled items.
**Action items:** prioritise fit tooling for Outerwear and Jeans (largest $ impact); review the returns policy globally.
author: analytics-team

question: Which acquisition channels bring the most valuable customers?
sql: SELECT u.traffic_source, COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 2) AS revenue_per_customer, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id), 2) AS aov FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY revenue DESC
report:
**Revenue by acquisition channel (users.traffic_source, net of cancels/returns).**
- Search dominates volume: 46.2k customers and $5.59M revenue (~70% of total).
- Customer *quality* is the same across channels: revenue per customer $120-$122 and AOV $85-$87 everywhere. Channels differ in reach, not in customer value.
**Interpretation rules used:** compare channels on revenue per customer and AOV, not totals; traffic_source is the channel at sign-up (first touch).
**Action items:** allocate budget on cost per acquisition (not in this dataset; join with marketing spend), since value per customer is channel-agnostic.
author: analytics-team

question: Which product categories are the most profitable?
sql: SELECT p.department, p.category, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost), 2) AS gross_profit, ROUND(100 * SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost) / SUM(oi.sale_price), 1) AS gross_margin_pct FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY gross_profit DESC LIMIT 10
report:
**Gross profit by department and category (net of cancels/returns).**
- Men's Outerwear & Coats is the profit leader ($350k gross profit, 55.9% margin), followed by Men's Suits & Sport Coats ($296k, 59.9%).
- Jeans is a volume driver with below-average margin (Men 46.8%, Women 45.8%): third in profit despite being second in revenue.
- Sleep & Lounge (Men) has the best margin in the top 10 (60.0%).
**Interpretation rules used:** gross profit = sale_price - products.cost per item; margin = profit / revenue. Revenue rankings and profit rankings differ: always show both.
**Action items:** price review for Jeans; promote high-margin Suits and Sleep & Lounge.
author: analytics-team

question: What is our repeat purchase rate and is customer loyalty improving?
sql: WITH per_customer AS ( SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders, MIN(created_at) AS first_order FROM orders WHERE status != 'Cancelled' GROUP BY 1) SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM first_order) AS cohort_year, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(100 * COUNTIF(orders >= 2) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_rate_pct, ROUND(AVG(orders), 2) AS avg_orders FROM per_customer GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
report:
**Repeat-purchase rate by first-order cohort (non-cancelled orders).**
- Older cohorts show higher repeat rates (2019: 53.5%) than newer ones (2025: 30.1%; 2026: 21.9%), but newer cohorts have had less time to come back: **compare cohorts at the same age** (e.g. repeat within 180 days of first order) before concluding loyalty is declining.
- Avg orders per customer falls from 1.86 (2019 cohort) to 1.29 (2026), consistent with cohort age.
**Interpretation rules used:** cohort = year of first non-cancelled order; repeat = 2+ orders. Cohort comparisons must be age-normalised.
**Action items:** track 90/180-day repeat rate per monthly cohort as the loyalty KPI.
author: analytics-team

question: How fast are we shipping and delivering orders?
sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS month, ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(shipped_at, created_at, HOUR)) / 24, 2) AS days_to_ship, ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(delivered_at, shipped_at, HOUR)) / 24, 2) AS days_in_transit, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders FROM orders WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 6 MONTH)) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
report:
**Fulfilment speed, last 6 months (delivered orders).**
- Order-to-ship time is stable at ~1.5 days; transit time ~2.4-2.5 days, so ~4 days door-to-door.
- Volume nearly doubled (1,274 to 2,272 delivered orders/month, Apr-Sep) with no degradation in speed: fulfilment is scaling.
**Interpretation rules used:** days_to_ship = shipped_at - created_at; transit = delivered_at - shipped_at; only orders with delivered_at.
**Action items:** none urgent; set an SLA alert if days_to_ship exceeds 2.0.
author: analytics-team

question: What are our best-selling products year to date?
sql: SELECT p.name AS product, p.brand, p.category, COUNT(*) AS units, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS ytd_revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') AND DATE(oi.created_at) >= DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR) GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY ytd_revenue DESC LIMIT 10
report:
**Top products by year-to-date net revenue (Jan 1 to today).**
- Premium outerwear dominates: The North Face (Nuptse 2, Apex Bionic) and Canada Goose take the top 5 slots; the #1 product made $6.3k from just 7 units.
- Units per product are low (3-7): revenue is driven by price point, not volume. Some products appear under more than one category (catalogue duplication): group by product name if exact totals matter.
**Interpretation rules used:** YTD = created_at >= DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR); exclude cancelled/returned items.
**Action items:** ensure stock depth on top outerwear SKUs; clean duplicate catalogue entries.
author: analytics-team

question: How does spending differ by age group and gender?
sql: SELECT CASE WHEN u.age < 25 THEN '18-24' WHEN u.age < 35 THEN '25-34' WHEN u.age < 45 THEN '35-44' WHEN u.age < 55 THEN '45-54' ELSE '55+' END AS age_band, u.gender, COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 2) AS spend_per_customer, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id), 2) AS aov FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2
report:
**Spend per customer by age band and gender (net).**
- Men spend ~13-16% more per customer than women in every age band (e.g. 25-34: $131 vs $113), driven by higher AOV (~$91 vs ~$80), not frequency.
- Age matters little: spend per customer is flat across bands ($112-$131). The 55+ band is the largest (17.8k customers).
**Interpretation rules used:** age bands 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55+; gender from users; never show individual customers.
**Action items:** test higher-ticket bundles for women's categories to close the AOV gap; do not over-invest in age targeting.
